summary: Defines metrics for the pattern of packet loss on a one-way Internet path, not just the overall loss rate. Two paths with equal loss rates can feel very different to users of real-time voice and video if their losses are bursty.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3357 measures how packet losses are spread along a path, not only how many there are. It defines two derived measurements: the distance between two lost packets, and a period of losses that starts after a packet arrived normally. Statistics built on those two measurements show whether a path loses packets now and then or loses them in bursts.

questions: how to measure packet loss patterns
why does bursty packet loss matter
subtitle: Measurements that describe the pattern of packet loss, not only the rate

tldr.problem: A loss rate on its own says little about what a path is like to use. Two paths with the same rate can feel very different, because one may scatter its losses while the other loses many packets in a row.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC derives two metrics from the base one-way loss metric: loss distance, the spacing between successive lost packets, and loss period, a run of losses that starts after a packet arrived normally. Four statistics computed from those streams summarise how noticeable the losses are and how bursty they are.
tldr.outcome: Operators and application developers can separate scattered loss from bursty loss, which is what decides how voice and video sound and how far a TCP throughput model is from reality.

facts.label: Statistics defined
facts.value: 4: noticeable rate, period total, period lengths, inter-period lengths

today: RFC 3357 is an Informational memo published in August 2002, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines derived metrics for the Internet Performance Metrics framework, so it remains a description of how to measure the shape of packet loss rather than a protocol to deploy.

sections.title: Why the Loss Rate Is Not Enough
sections.content:
For real-time applications such as packet voice and video, the pattern of loss is a key parameter in the performance users observe. For the same loss rate, two different loss distributions could produce very different perceptions of performance. The impact of the loss pattern is equally important for non-real-time applications that use an adaptive protocol such as TCP.

The Internet Performance Metrics work had previously concentrated on base metrics such as delay, loss and connectivity, under the framework described in RFC 2330. This document captures one specific Internet behaviour, the packet loss process, in the same framework by defining derived metrics. The loss period metric captures the frequency and length, that is the burstiness, of loss once it starts, and the loss distance metric captures the spacing between the loss periods. Both are derived from the base metric Type-P-One-Way-packet-Loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Two networks can lose the same share of packets and feel very different to the people using them. This document measures how the losses are spread out, not only how many there are.

sections.title: Loss Distance and Loss Period
sections.content:
The document defines the terms it uses. Bursty loss is loss involving consecutive packets of a stream. Loss distance is the difference in sequence numbers of two successively lost packets, which may or may not be separated by successfully received packets: if the packet with sequence number 20 is lost and the next lost packet is number 50, the loss distance is 30. The sequence numbers are consecutive integers across the packets of a time series sample, and the document does not specify exactly how they are associated with packets. They could be carried inside the test packets or derived afterwards.

A loss period begins when a lost packet follows a received one. Writing f(P_i) as 1 for a lost packet and 0 for a received one, a loss period begins where f(P_i) is 1 and f(P_(i-1)) is 0. In the sample of received and lost packets r r r x r r x x x r x r r x x x there are four loss periods, beginning at P_3, P_6, P_10 and P_13.
sections.plainLanguage: Two measurements describe the pattern. The loss distance is how far apart two lost packets are, counted in packet numbers. A loss period is a run of losses that starts after a packet arrived normally.

sections.title: The Two Derived Streams
sections.content:
Both derived metrics are defined over a base Type-P-One-Way-Loss-Stream, a sequence of pairs of time and loss. The loss distance stream is a sequence of pairs of loss distance and loss. When a packet is lost, its loss distance is the difference between its sequence number and that of the previously lost packet, and the loss distance of the very first loss in the sample is zero.

The loss period stream is a sequence of pairs of loss period and loss. A counter starting at zero is incremented each time a loss period begins. The loss period is set to zero when the packet was received, and to the counter value when the packet was lost, so the counter says which loss period each lost packet belongs to.

The worked example uses the base sample {<T1,0>,<T2,1>,<T3,0>,<T4,0>,<T5,1>,<T6,0>,<T7,1>,<T8,0>,<T9,1>,<T10,1>}, in which the packets sent at T2, T5, T7, T9 and T10 are lost. The loss distance stream is {<0,0>,<0,1>,<0,0>,<0,0>,<3,1>,<0,0>,<2,1>,<0,0>,<2,1>,<1,1>}, because the distances are 0 for the first loss, then 5-2, 2 and 1. The loss period stream is {<0,0>,<1,1>,<0,0>,<0,0>,<2,1>,<0,0>,<3,1>,<0,0>,<4,1>,<4,1>}, because the packet at T10 continues the fourth period rather than starting a fifth.
sections.plainLanguage: Each measurement turns the list of lost and received packets into a list of pairs. One pair says how far the loss was from the previous loss, the other says which run of losses it belonged to.

sections.title: Statistics Computed From the Streams
sections.content:
Four statistics summarise the two streams.

  • The Loss-Noticeable-Rate counts the losses whose distance from the previous loss is no greater than a chosen limit, called the loss constraint delta, and divides by the number of losses. It is useful when the distance between successive losses matters. Many multimedia codecs can conceal the effect of a loss by using past history, and that ability degrades when the history is poor because the losses are close together, so choosing delta on the basis of this sensitivity measures how noticeable a loss might be.
  • The Loss-Period-Total is the largest loss period number in the loss period stream, so it counts the loss periods. It does not describe the duration of any one period, so a large value does not mean the losses are spread out: one or more periods may contain bursty losses.
  • The Loss-Period-Lengths gives, for each period, the number of packets lost in it, which is the indicator of burstiness.
  • The Inter-Loss-Period-Lengths gives the distance between the last packet lost in one period and the first packet lost in the next, so two periods separated by a short distance can be treated as belonging to the same burst.

In the worked example, with delta equal to 2, three of the five losses break the limit, so the noticeable rate is 3/5. The loss period total is 4, the period lengths are 1, 1, 1 and 2, and the inter-period lengths are {<1,0>,<2,3>,<3,2>,<4,2>}.
sections.plainLanguage: Four numbers summarise the pattern: how many losses are close enough together to matter, how many runs of loss there were, how many packets each run lost, and how far apart the runs were.

sections.title: How a Measurement Is Made
sections.content:
The measurement uses the same methodology as the base one-way loss metric. The sending and receiving hosts have clocks synchronised with each other, and the degree of synchronisation is a parameter of the methodology that depends on the threshold used to decide that a packet is lost.

At the sending host, the source and destination IP addresses are selected and a Type-P test packet is formed with them. The receiving host is arranged to receive the packet, and the sending host puts a timestamp in the prepared packet and sends it towards the destination. If the packet arrives within a reasonable period of time, the one-way packet loss is taken to be zero; if it fails to arrive within that period, the loss is taken to be one. The threshold of reasonable is a parameter of the methodology.

The metrics can be used with any sampling method. The document warns that Poisson sampling may not yield appropriate values for these metrics for real-time applications such as voice over IP, or for TCP-based applications, and suggests the ON-OFF model for real-time work. In that model an ON period starts with a certain probability p, during which a certain number of packets are transmitted with a mean of lambda-on according to a geometric distribution, and an OFF period starts with probability 1-p and lasts for a period of time based on an exponential distribution with rate lambda-off.
sections.plainLanguage: One host sends timestamped test packets to another and records which ones arrive. A packet that does not arrive in time counts as lost. How often the packets are sent, and how long they may take, are choices the tester makes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies metrics rather than a protocol, so it does not directly affect the security of the Internet or of applications running on it. Implementations of the metrics must still be mindful of security and privacy. The derived metrics inherit the security considerations of the base loss metric in RFC 2680, and the reader is pointed there for the full treatment.

Three points are raised. The lambda that controls the rate at which test packets are sent must be chosen carefully: if it is set inappropriately large it could perturb the network under test, cause congestion, or at worst amount to a denial-of-service attack against that network. Legitimate measurements therefore have to pick their parameters so that they do not interfere with normal traffic.

Privacy is not a concern, because the test packets contain no user information, and even if packets did contain user information the derived metrics do not release data sent by the user. Results could be perturbed by corrupting or disrupting the underlying stream, for example by adding extra packets that look just like test packets, so packet authentication and integrity checks such as a signed cryptographic hash MAY be used to confirm that the test packets are valid and unaltered.
sections.plainLanguage: A measurement that sends packets too fast can congest the network it is testing. The test packets carry no user data, but someone could add fake test packets to distort the result, so the packets can be signed to prove they are genuine.

items.label: Spacing
items.desc: The difference in sequence numbers between two successively lost packets. The first loss in a sample has a distance of zero.

items.label: Run of losses
items.desc: A run of lost packets that begins when a lost packet follows a received one.

items.label: Closeness
items.desc: The share of losses whose distance from the previous loss is no greater than the loss constraint delta.

items.label: Number of runs
items.desc: The largest loss period number in the loss period stream, so it counts the loss periods.

items.label: Burstiness
items.desc: The number of packets lost in each loss period.

items.label: Spacing between runs
items.desc: The distance between the last packet lost in one period and the first packet lost in the next.
